pages.transcript:
Post Unit News
[AFL-CIO seal] Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild
No. 103 -/ Date December 3, 198[7]

EQUALITY AND JUSTICE, POST STYLE

Post Unit News seems to have nothing but readers whenever we put together a listing of Post salaries. Last May we told you about salaries for full-time employees covered by the Guild contract as of October, 1986. Now we've got similar data as of September's payroll-- after the company illegally declared an impasse in contract talks and unilaterally imposed its final wage offer.

As you can see, the latest raises have only widened the pay disparity for people doing the same jobs. This enormous range of salaries shows all the more how subjective the system of compensation has become during the years since The Post instituted a dual pay system here.

Some of the higher-paid employees at The Post have climbed the salary list through longevity, as beneficiaries of general pay increases handed out to the workforce over the years but not applied to the contract minimums. Others among the higher-paid are newer, so-called "fast track" employees who have been given merit raises to surpass what many of their colleagues are earning. Women and black employees do much worse than others, on average.

The lower-paid employees in any job classification are the real victims of The Post's unfair pay system. They earn less not through any fault or failure on their part, but because of the unfair, discriminatory system imposed by the publisher a decade ago to boost profits. The result, an absurd array of pay for the same jobs, is printed below.

documents.title: Confidential comparator narrative — John Yang
documents.subject: The Washington Post's compensation explanation for comparator John Yang (background, starting salary, salary history, explanation) in the salary-difference narratives prepared for the Hamilton arbitration, relative to Skrzycki
documents.date: circa 2002 (same series as the batch-9 comparator narratives, which reference September 1, 2002 snapshots)
documents.notes: Single typed page headed 'CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES / PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES' — the same document family as batch 9's Fromson/Gillis/Goodman/Segal/Smart narratives. The narrative is complete on this page (it ends with the 'Explanation' paragraph).

pages.transcript:
CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION UNDER THE AGREED ARBITRATION PROCEDURES
PREPARED FOR SETTLEMENT PURPOSES

John Yang

John Yang was paid slightly more than Skrzycki on the 1998 salary snapshot.

Background:
John Yang came to The Post in the early 1990s as a reporter in National. He became an Assignment Editor in Financial News in 1992, returning to National as a reporter in 1995. He became an Assignment Editor in Style in 1998, moving to Financial News as a reporter later that year. In 1999, he became the Director of Recruiting. He left The Post later that year. Prior to starting at The Post, Yang worked as a reporter at The Wall Street Journal for almost four years. He also spent approximately five years as a correspondent for Time Magazine and one year as a staff writer for the Boston Globe. Yang is a graduate Wesleyan University.

Starting Salary:
Upon starting at The Post, Yang received approximately a 14 percent increase over his prior salary. His starting salary was slightly less than the salary of Skrzycki at that time.

Salary History
Yang received one merit increase during his time at The Post - which he received as a reporter in National. Yang received a salary increase when he became an Assignment Editor in Financial News in 1992. He also received a salary increase when he became Director of Recruiting in 1999.

Explanation:

Yang previously held key positions at The Post, such as White House correspondent, resulting in a merit increase while he was in National. He came to Financial News as an Assignment Editor. He retained his editor's salary when he became a reporter in Financial News.

documents.title: Post Unit News No. 18 — Special Bulletin: EEO Settlement (1972 class sex-discrimination complaint)
documents.subject: Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild bulletin describing the settlement of the class action sex discrimination complaint against The Washington Post (complaint filed June 19, 1974 covering women employed at least six months between May 29, 1972 and that date), including release/compensation amounts and the good-faith goals for women in editorial and commercial jobs
documents.notes: Mimeographed newsletter page, masthead 'Post Unit News / Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild / No. 18 / Date December 2, 1980', marked '(more)' at lower right, so this is only the first page of the bulletin. Historically significant for the Hamilton case: it documents the earlier Post sex-discrimination settlement and its women-in-jobs goals.

pages.transcript:
Post Unit News
[AFL-CIO seal] Washington/Baltimore Newspaper Guild
No. 18   Date December 2, 1980

SPECIAL BULLETIN — EEO SETTLEMENT

Within the next month, our lawyers will be asking Guild employees who signed a class action sex discrimination complaint filed against the newspaper eight years ago to sign off on a settlement with the Post announced last week. The agreement, to be monitored by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, does not go into effect until the more than 100 charging parties say they accept it.

Persons who filed the complaint are urged to sign the agreement as soon as they are contacted. Once the agreement is formalized, our lawyers will have three months to try to contact and obtain signed releases from members of the class - the more than 550 women who were working at the Post at least six months between May 29, 1972, when the complaint was filed, and June 19, 1974, when the EEOC found that the complaint was justified. If you worked here at that period, whether or not you signed the complaint, you are a member of the class. Releases from 95 per cent of those who can be located have to be returned before the agreement goes into effect.

Women who sign releases will be eligible for the following compensation, depending on how long they were employed:

up to 1 year.....$ 50
1 to 2 years.....100
2 to 3 years.....175
3 to 4 years.....250

Summary of the agreement and copies of the entire settlement are being mailed to charging parties. Here are some other provisions:

* The Post will make a "good faith effort" over the next five years to fill one-third of the officials, managers and professional jobs in news and editorial that become available with women. In some departments, the goals will be different: Metro's goal is 40 per cent of the jobs that open up; Sports, 20 per cent; Style, 40 per cent. A third of all assignment editor, critic and columnist jobs, excluding copy editors, are to be offered to women.

* This same "good faith effort" will be made to fill a third of the job openings for managers in combined commercial departments with women. The specific goal for officials and managers in Accounting is 35 per cent; Administration, 25 per cent; Advertising, 33.3 per cent; Circulation, 15 per cent. One-third of the professional jobs opening up in commercial are to go to women, with goals of 35 per cent for Administration and Advertising. In addition, a goal of 45 per cent is set for outside sales persons in Advertising.

* Job vacancies will be posted at the employment office and on bulletin boards. Any employee denied a vacant position can ask to be given the reasons and the steps needed to qualify - in writing.

* A woman who believes that her title and salary do not compensate her for her duties and responsibilities may request a change in classification and salary within 30 days after the effective date of the agreement. She may make this request directly to Publisher Donald Graham, or, if she prefers, to the personnel director, the manager of employment and affirmative action or the assistant managing editor for personnel, who shall make recommendations to the publisher. The employee may have another employee accompany her. If the request is in writing, the response will be in writing. We will have more about this in a later bulletin.

* The Post says it will "expand its general training and career development activities in all Commercial departments" over the next five years and make them "available to all women on a nondiscriminatory basis." The current summer and two-year internship programs in the newsroom will also continue, with 40 per cent of the positions aimed at women.

* During the next five years, the Post will offer three scholarships and two sabbaticals to women employees for'up to one year, to study journalism, business, commercial art or data processing. The women have to have been employed at the Post

(more)

Affiliated with American Federation of Labor-Congress of Industrial Organizations, Canadian Labour Congress.

documents.title: Guild handout: 'Average Salaries Show Patterns of Discrimination' (key-minimum salary comparisons by race and sex), with the Guild's discrimination-charge statement signed by Unit Chair Jill Neilson
documents.subject: Typewitted Guild bargaining-unit statement showing average Post salaries by race and sex within key classifications (managers/editors, assistant and assignment editors, copy editors, reporters, columnists/critics, photographers, outside sales, artists/copy writers/layout, T-5 data programmer), the $664.35 'key minimum' rate covering 559 full-time employees, and the closing grounds of the Guild's race/sex discrimination charge filed with the D.C. Office of Human Rights
documents.date: approx. late 1987 - early 1988 (undated; references the impasse/final-offer period, a byline strike, a May vote to file the charge, and publisher Donald Graham — consistent with Post Unit News No. 103 of December 3, 1987)
documents.notes: Two consecutive typewitted pages in the batch (visibly the same typeface/paper, unlike the mimeographed newsletters) that belong to one argument: the first page presents the average-salary breakdown 'AVERAGE SALARIES SHOW PATTERNS OF DISCRIMINATION' ending mid-table at 'T-5 DATA PROGRAMMER'; the second page opens mid-list with the tail of a numbered statement of discrimination grounds ('Black women are devastated by both race and sex discrimination...') followed by ground '4.' and the closing call to action signed '-- Jill Neilson, Unit Chair'. Logical reading order is 3FCCF507 (salary averages) then 3ECFFF9F (charge text/close); pages numbered here in batch filename order, so pageNumber 1 below is actually the second physical page of the handout. Not merged with DOC-001 because production method and document identity differ, though the two are almost certainly the same campaign/materials. 'Do[n] Graham' in the last paragraph appears to be typed as 'Dom Graham' and is left as seen rather than corrected.

pages.transcript:
Black women are devastated by both race and sex discrimination. On average, black women reporters earn $172.00 a week less than white males of similar age and tenure. Of all other workers who are not reporters, black women earn an average of $212.00 less than white men.

4. That The Post relies on subjective judgment in setting merit pay. Its failure to establish objective, nondiscriminatory job-related criteria has led to fewer and lesser merit increases for women, blacks and other minorities.

The Guild has attempted to address the issue of discrimination with Post management, to no avail. We have tried to set our house in order. The Post has refused to cooperate.

Today, we have asked for assistance from the D.C. Office of Human Rights. This office has the authority to subpoena information from management, the same information management has consistently refused to release to the Guild. This office will investigate the charges, attempt conciliation if they are substantiated and, if conciliation fails, arrange a hearing before the D.C. Commission on Human Rights. (If you have information which might interest the Office of Human Rights, you can contact attorney/investigator Jeffery Tacy directly at (202) 939-8740.)

In May of this year, Guild members voted overwhelmingly to file the discrimination charge. We are confident that the elimination of discrimination at The Post will benefit everyone who works at The Post. Creating an environment in which all workers are treated fairly will inevitably make this great paper a greater one. We look forward to the day when we will be judged by the content of our work and not by our skin, age or sex.

THE MESSAGE IS CLEAR!

Thanks to all who despite management's attempts to make the last two days agonizing and unpleasant for many ---oops! Thanks to all of you who participated in the byline strike, a rousing success, contrary to management's mixed messages.

Withholding your byline sends a message not only to management, but to other workers and our readership that all is not well at The Washington Post.

Employees in the Commercial Dept. are circulating a petition urging management to "return to the bargaining table and negotiate in good faith so that we can all enjoy a fair contract and a more harmonious workplace." We appreciate their support. We will attempt to present the petition to Do[n] Graham today.

-- Jill Neilson, Unit Chair

AVERAGE SALARIES SHOW PATTERNS OF DISCRIMINATION

The pattern of discrimination is clearest in the "key minimum" positions, which cover 559 fulltime employees. The "key minimum" positions are those that pay the highest salary under the contract (except for positions that carry percentage differentials on top of salary). The current "key minimum"-- or top rate of pay -- for the positions listed below is $664.35. Few people are paid at that rate which has allowed the Post a free hand to set salaries.
